newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish economy heads for higher deficits in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Turkish economy heads for higher deficits in 1996.

text.p: Turkey's central bank governor Gazi Ercel predicted on Friday the economy would face higher deficits this year, amid increased uncertainty over the future of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist-led government.

"The current account deficit is estimated to rise to $6-$7 billion this year," Ercel told Reuters. He said the public sector borrowing requirement was expected to reach nine to 10 percent of gross national product after 6.5 percent in 1995.
The current account deficit was $2.3 billion last year. Economists say this year's deficit may exceed the previous record of $6.4 billion recorded in 1993.
Despite the alarming figures, bankers say the central bank's policies and high foreign exchange reserves would ensure short-term stability in financial markets.

Ercel says unregistered hard currency earnings of $5 to $10 billion help Turkey finance its current account deficit, referring to the so-called "suitcase" trade by East Europeans, Russians and Central Asians who come to Turkey as tourists but buy Turkish products, mainly textile goods for resale back home.
The government has yet to unveil any definite plans to contain huge deficits and curb chronic inflation running at around 80 percent.
Instead, it is struggling to survive as the opposition steps up its campaign to topple the government after Erbakan's controversial trip to Libya last week.
Parliament will debate a censure motion against Erbakan next week, coinciding with a visit by a team from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to examine the economy and 1997 targets.
Economists and economic bureaucrats have urged the government to reach an accord with the IMF for a new stand-by credit arrangement.
But Erbakan's Welfare Party, which advocated populist and anti-western economic policies for decades, has not signalled yet that it would consent to a deal with the IMF.

"Turkey must settle its relations with the IMF on an official frame," Ercel said, adding that the Fund would ask Turkey to improve its fiscal balance, reform the loss-making pension system and accelerate privatisation.
Turkey is expected to draw up a new economic action plan after the IMF visit.
Western bankers said Turkey's credibility in international markets would be hampered unless it puts a serious programme into practice under IMF surveillance.
Economists fear that any tightening in western fund flows and downgrading of the coutry's already-low investment grade by rating agencies could spark a crisis.

An IMF-advised programme, on the other hand, may face tough opposition from workers if it envisages lowering real wage levels and raising public sector prices as Turkey did in 1994 under another IMF-monitored plan.

This may also weaken the popularity of Welfare, which won millions of new supporters and became the biggest political party in elections last December in part due to anti-IMF and populist policies and pledges over the past five years.

"This is the most critical dilemma of Erbakan. He will lose his popularity if Turkey reaches an accord with the IMF or the economy will sink further if Turkey doesn't," a senior economy official said.

"Or he might tend to win more time by delaying the implementation of a severe economic package and occupying the country's agenda with soft and unrealistic economic measures, and go for elections next year," the official added.
Ercel said Turkey should design a medium-term economic plan aimed at lowering inflation.

"Now the markets are calm. They can see the outlook in the coming three months and there is very good dialogue among the central bank, markets and the treasury. But the outlook in people's mind should be extended," Ercel said.
